claims.text: Low-temperature cyclic loading that produces localized plastic deformation causes kinetic segregation of minor atomic species to grain boundaries in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy.
Stress-induced grain-boundary segregation forms a thin amorphous or interfacial complexion phase.
The proposed grain-boundary complexion is inherently brittle.
The brittle complexion degrades toughness without nucleation of conventional intermetallic particles.
The initial alloy is single phase and has a homogeneous elemental distribution with no pre-existing segregated or precipitated phases.
Low-temperature cyclic tensile or fatigue loading promotes dislocation pile-ups.
Localized stresses near grain boundaries drive selected atoms to diffuse to those interfaces under the imposed loading conditions.
Stress-driven segregation creates compositionally heterogeneous grain boundaries.
The compositionally heterogeneous grain boundaries have reduced cohesive strength.
Reduced grain-boundary cohesive strength triggers brittle failure instead of the baseline ductile response.
Cyclically loaded samples will have lower fracture toughness than an undeformed control held at the same temperature.
Cyclically loaded samples will exhibit enriched grain-boundary regions detectable by atom probe tomography or high-resolution STEM-EDS.
No detectable bulk intermetallic precipitation will accompany the predicted toughness degradation.
The as-processed, undeformed alloy has favorable strength–ductility behavior and high fracture toughness under standard service conditions.
The proposed mechanism is limited to low-temperature cyclic or fatigue loading that induces plastic deformation while preserving the bulk single-phase microstructure.
